section_summary: This section documents U.S., British, Canadian, and other Allied concern over strategic materials reaching Japan through direct exports, transshipment, or third-country intermediaries. It covers cobalt, zinc, mercury, vanadium, tin, scrap iron, steel, petroleum, aviation gasoline, mica, rubber, hides, and other commodities, alongside investigations, intelligence reports, export-control correspondence, and public demands for a broader embargo. The papers also address aid to China, British economic pressure on Japan, Japanese-Soviet negotiations, and commodity movements through Latin America and Southeast Asia.

subfiles.title: Referral to the Treasury of the Canadian cobalt-shipment inquiry
subfiles.from: Adolf A. Berle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Henry Morgenthau Jr., Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Requests an investigation of cobalt products shipped from Canada to the United States and apparently reshipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department forwards Vincent Armstrong's letter and a Canadian Legation communication concerning a cobalt shipment. It asks the Treasury to determine whether the transaction involved any breach of good faith.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment and referral of cobalt inquiry
subfiles.from: Herbert E. Gaston, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Reports that the cobalt case has been sent to the supervising customs agent in New York for investigation.
subfiles.summary: Gaston acknowledges the State Department's confidential communication of November 27. He states that the papers were referred to the supervising customs agent at New York and promises a further report when the investigation is completed.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning Spanish mercury destined for Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether Argentine law could be used to seize Spanish mercury and redirect it to Western Hemisphere defense consumers.
subfiles.summary: The Department argues that mercury is urgently needed in the United States and other American republics and should be kept from Japan. It asks whether Argentina can lawfully seize the shipment, whether doing so is politically expedient, and notes that the Metals Reserve Corporation is prepared to negotiate a purchase.

subfiles.title: Letter urging greater aid to China and further restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States continues to supply Japan with war materials and urges stronger support for China.
subfiles.summary: The writer thanks Hull for past efforts to aid China but argues that more assistance is urgently needed. Three questions challenge continued Japanese access to American materials, the failure to broaden embargoes despite public support, and the security implications of Japan's alliance with the Axis.

subfiles.title: Senator Taft's inquiry concerning a shortage of slab zinc
subfiles.about: Forwards a Cincinnati company's request for a temporary embargo on exports of slab zinc or spelter.
subfiles.summary: Taft quotes the F. H. Lawson Company, which reports an acute domestic shortage of spelter while Japan imported about 3,800 tons in October. The company says the shortage is hampering galvanized-goods production and the defense program, and Taft asks whether an embargo is contemplated.

subfiles.title: Referral of Senator Taft's zinc letter to Export Control
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards Senator Taft's letter about zinc exports to Japan for appropriate action.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the December 9 letter from Senator Taft concerning the F. H. Lawson Company's request for restrictions on zinc exports. He notes that Taft has been informed of the referral.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Taft concerning zinc exports
subfiles.about: Advises Taft that his zinc-export inquiry has been referred to the Administrator of Export Control.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Taft's letter quoting the F. H. Lawson Company. Because the Administrator of Export Control decides questions involving materials designated as essential to national defense, the letter has been sent there for consideration.

subfiles.title: Transfer sheet for file item 894.24/1177
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of a document to another decimal-file classification.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains only a notice that item 894.24/1177 was transferred to file 856D.6363/798. It preserves the filing trail but gives no substantive description of the transferred document.

subfiles.title: Exact amounts of contraband found at Manzanillo
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt, American Vice Consul, Manzanillo
subfiles.about: Reports the official quantities and value of metals seized in an attempted contraband shipment from Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: Hoyt follows up his October 9 despatch with figures supplied by the local customhouse under instructions from Mexico City. Although much of the OCR table is illegible, the reported total is 1,691,718 pesos, or $348,788.43; the goods will be fined, claimed by their owner, or sold at auction.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Butler's confidential communications
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of British information on exports, Southeast Asia, and Soviet-Japanese negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Butler's November 5 personal and confidential letter and its two enclosures. He specifically agrees to treat the portion concerning Soviet-Japanese negotiations as highly confidential.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter and notes on exports and Asian diplomacy
subfiles.about: Transmits confidential British intelligence on export restrictions, Thailand, Soviet-Japanese negotiations, and aircraft transport.
subfiles.summary: Butler forwards the substance of a Foreign Office telegram and asks that the Soviet-Japanese portion remain highly confidential. The notes describe British plans to restrict exports to Japan, Thai policy toward Indochina, reported Japanese negotiating proposals to Moscow involving Sakhalin, Manchuria, Dairen, Manchukuo, and aid to Chungking, and an inquiry about shipping twenty-one pursuit planes from Mexico to Bangkok or Singapore.

subfiles.title: Division of European Affairs routing memorandum
subfiles.to: Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Routes an attached memorandum whose substantive description is obscured by poor OCR.
subfiles.summary: The page is a State Department routing memorandum from the Division of European Affairs. Its central text indicates that an attached memorandum is being transmitted, but the subject and most wording are illegible.

subfiles.title: Canadian information on Stuart Hosie's proposed trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Records a Bogotá trader's proposal to export scrap iron and other Colombian products to Japan through reciprocal trade.
subfiles.summary: Canadian authorities report that Stuart Hosie approached the Fujiye Trading Company in Osaka, citing earlier experience exporting scrap iron to Germany. He offered scrap iron, coffee, vegetable ivory, and wood, provided that imports from Japan equaled the value of Colombia's exports, and the memorandum recommends keeping a record of him as a scrap-iron dealer.

subfiles.title: Colombian zinc production and proposed sale to Japan
subfiles.from: Canadian Legation information based on a letter from I. Okura
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Japanese-language letter about a high-grade zinc mine near Bogotá and possible sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: I. Okura reports a zinc deposit near Bogotá containing roughly 55–64 percent metal, with about 1,000 tons in storage and an owner willing to sell to Japan. The memorandum provides an assay and explains that high inland transport costs to Buenaventura had discouraged exports, while lower current ocean freight might make renewed sales possible.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Colombian zinc memorandum to Bogotá
subfiles.about: Sends the embassy a confidential copy of the Canadian memorandum on zinc production in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State encloses the memorandum received from the Canadian Legation. It is supplied strictly for the ambassador's information and the embassy's files.

subfiles.title: Elsie Sherwood's letter opposing exports of war materials
subfiles.about: Questions continued American exports of gasoline, oil, automobile parts, and other war materials to an aggressive power.
subfiles.summary: Sherwood asks how the United States can continue supplying an imperialistic nation that it may later have to confront. She doubts that exporting basic war materials to an eastern Axis partner reflects the will of the American people and invokes the danger faced by China and Britain.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting a draft reply to Elsie Sherwood
subfiles.about: Attaches a proposed response to Elsie Sherwood's November 18 letter.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that a draft reply has been prepared in compliance with a November 20 request. Routing initials identify Far Eastern Affairs staff participation in preparing the response.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles's November 28 reply to Elsie Sherwood
subfiles.about: Assures Sherwood that Far Eastern relations are receiving close attention and sends foreign-policy speeches.
subfiles.summary: Welles says Sherwood's questions are complex and that official pressures prevent a comprehensive correspondence. He assures her that relations with the Far East are under close review and encloses recent addresses by Cordell Hull and himself.

subfiles.title: Undated draft reply to Elsie Sherwood
subfiles.about: Drafts a general response to Sherwood without addressing her export-policy questions in detail.
subfiles.summary: The draft characterizes the questions as highly complex and says the government is closely examining its Far Eastern relations. It encloses Welles's Cleveland address of September 28 and the Secretary of State's Washington address of October 26.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles's November 25 reply to Elsie Sherwood
subfiles.about: Provides a polished response assuring Sherwood of attention to Far Eastern affairs.
subfiles.summary: Welles welcomes renewed contact with Sherwood but says her questions are too broad for a satisfactory detailed reply. He encloses recent foreign-policy addresses by Hull and himself as statements of the government's fundamental position.

subfiles.title: Alternate undated reply to Elsie Sherwood
subfiles.about: Offers another version of the general reply to Sherwood's concerns about the Far East.
subfiles.summary: This version again says that pressure of work prevents a comprehensive discussion and that the government is closely considering Far Eastern problems. It encloses Welles's Cleveland address and the Secretary of State's Washington address.

subfiles.title: Canadian Legation inquiry into cobalt concentrates diverted toward Japan
subfiles.to: B. T. Wailes, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests U.S. assistance tracing Canadian cobalt concentrates that may have been reshipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Canadian inquiries connected the suspicious shipment with approximately 203 tons of cobalt concentrates sold by Cobalt Products Limited to the Metal and Ore Corporation after an assurance that they were for U.S. consumption. Stirling Smith denied that the material had been re-exported, so the Legation asks whether U.S. authorities can inspect the purchaser's books and stocks or permit Canadian officials to do so.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on handling Vincent Armstrong's cobalt report
subfiles.about: Records the decision to pass Armstrong's cobalt allegations informally and confidentially to Canadian authorities.
subfiles.summary: After consultation with officials from several State Department divisions, Wailes concluded that the Department could do no more than communicate Armstrong's information informally to Canada. Macdonnell of the Canadian Legation was allowed to read the letter with a warning that its claims were unverified, and he thought Ottawa might use it in monitoring future shipments.

subfiles.title: Request to verify Brazilian mica-export statistics
subfiles.from: Department of State, transmitting a National Defense Commission request
subfiles.about: Seeks confirmation or correction of apparently inconsistent figures for Brazilian mica exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Successive despatches reported 78,000 kilograms for six months, 418,000 kilograms for July, and 531,000 kilograms for nine months. Because the July figure appears difficult to reconcile with the cumulative totals, the embassy is asked to cable corrected figures.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal on aviation gasoline dealings
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential information about contemplated oil and aviation-gasoline dealings involving Mitsui, Cities Service, and B. T. McNeil.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle a memorandum derived from a confidential source. The source indicates past and prospective transactions in aviation gasoline and other petroleum products between Mitsui, Cities Service, and McNeil.

subfiles.title: FBI memorandum reproducing oil-shipment telegrams
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr. and State Department files
subfiles.about: Summarizes intercepted or obtained telegrams concerning gasoline, aviation fuel, lubricating oil, and related shipments arranged by Mitsui.
subfiles.summary: The telegrams detail proposed and accepted loadings of motor gasoline, leaded aviation gasoline, and lubricating oil aboard several vessels, with quantities commonly stated in drums. Additional messages concern sesame seed at Manzanillo, completed gasoline loading at New Orleans, loading at St. Rose, and negotiations with N. G. Wood in New York.

subfiles.title: Charles Noble's appeal for a stronger embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: Urges stricter enforcement of the embargo on war supplies to Japan and larger loans to China.
subfiles.summary: Noble contends that goods on the embargoed list are still leaking through to Japan. Identifying himself as an American citizen opposed to international aggression, he also requests increased financial assistance to the Chinese government.

subfiles.title: Rangoon report on gasoline withdrawals and shipment delays
subfiles.about: Reports authorized gasoline withdrawals and the resumption of shipments after railway repairs.
subfiles.summary: Weekly gasoline withdrawals were authorized in amounts corresponding to loadings, and 972 drums had been prepared for dispatch. Railway damage delayed movement, but repairs allowed shipments to resume on October 29; withdrawals of up to 8,000 drums were being authorized, with 74 drums retained to cover leakage shortages.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on an American Legion boycott resolution
subfiles.from: American Legion, Department of Vermont, Waldo H. Heinrichs
subfiles.about: Points to a letter advocating an expanded and total boycott of Japan to restrain aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes a Vermont American Legion communication supporting stronger economic action against Japan. It directs researchers to the original letter in file 841.24/353.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Greek ships carrying scrap iron to Japan
subfiles.about: References a British Embassy note concerning Greek vessels arriving in Japan with scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: The sheet states that the original note enclosed a telegram received from London. The underlying subject was the arrival in Japan of Greek ships carrying scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japan's iron and steel industry
subfiles.about: References a Justice Department letter enclosing memoranda on the Japanese iron and steel industry.
subfiles.summary: The original letter transmitted copies of memoranda concerning iron and steel production in Japan. The sheet redirects the reader to file 894.6351/.2.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on British economic pressure against Japan
subfiles.from: American diplomatic mission in Great Britain, Herschel V. Johnson
subfiles.about: References confidential information on British plans to apply economic pressure to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram 3835 from Great Britain. Its subject is British government planning for economic measures against Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Panamanian-registry vessels transferred to Japan
subfiles.about: References a telegram seeking Panamanian cooperation against transfers of vessels to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference concerns ships under Panamanian registry that were being transferred to Japan. The cited telegram explained the U.S. attitude and asked whether Panama would cooperate in preventing future transfers.

subfiles.title: British Embassy commodity-movement notes for Latin America
subfiles.about: Provides intelligence on strategic commodity movements through Latin America, including possible diversion of U.S. goods to Japan through Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Thorold supplies notes intended to complement information collected by Spaeth's committee and highlights Mexican consignments to Manchukuo containing materials not evidently produced in Mexico. The enclosures list metals proposed or shipped through Mexico; Japanese and German purchases of Brazilian castor seed; credits for German wool firms in Uruguay; additional Brazilian shipments; purchases in Peru; rubber shipments to Vladivostok and Moscow; and a sharp rise in Japanese hide purchases from Buenos Aires. The notes suggest that Mexico may be acting as an entrepôt for U.S. exports and that some nominally Japanese purchases in Brazil were actually for Germany.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Thorold's Latin American trade notes
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the British Embassy's material on Latin American export movements.
subfiles.summary: Feis thanks Thorold for the January 18 letter and its enclosures. He notes that copies of the same material had also been sent to Spaeth.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal on a suspected cobalt purchase
subfiles.about: Forwards information that unidentified buyers in New York may be seeking cobalt for shipment to Japan or Germany.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends a memorandum based on a confidential informant's report. The information concerns an attempted purchase of cobalt, a material of major importance to war industry, under circumstances suggesting ultimate delivery to Japan or Germany.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on cobalt routed through Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports a suspected plan to send Canadian cobalt through New York and Mexico to Japan or Germany.
subfiles.summary: An informant reports market inquiries for ten tons of cobalt ostensibly intended for Mexican government consumption. The cobalt was reportedly purchased in Canada at $2.49 per pound and scheduled to travel through New York and Mexico, although the informant believed Mexico could not use that quantity and that Japan or Germany was the true destination.

subfiles.title: Coast Guard transmittal of shipping-intelligence summaries
subfiles.from: L. T. Chalker, United States Coast Guard
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence summaries on Japanese cargoes and the German steamship Pauline Friederich.
subfiles.summary: Chalker sends two confidential attachments for Saugstad's information and any action he considers appropriate. The enclosures cover cargoes loaded by Japanese vessels and a proposed sale of the German ship Pauline Friederich.

subfiles.title: Cargoes loaded by Japanese vessels at New Orleans
subfiles.to: Treasury, Customs, State Department, Naval Intelligence, and Merchant Ship Control
subfiles.about: Lists petroleum cargoes taken by Japanese ships departing New Orleans between July and December 1940.
subfiles.summary: The report observes that Japanese vessels were taking gasoline, crude oil, and lubricating oil in metal drums rather than chiefly in bulk, with the drums apparently sold with their contents and not intended for return. It lists vessels, destinations, sailing dates, and cargo quantities for departures from July 17 through December 4, 1940.

subfiles.title: Proposed sale of the German steamship Pauline Friederich
subfiles.to: Treasury, Customs, State Department, Naval Intelligence, and Merchant Ship Control
subfiles.about: Reports an effort to offer a German vessel for sale because of fears that Axis ships might be seized in American ports.
subfiles.summary: The John G. Hall Company of Boston was reportedly approached about selling the Pauline Friederich, with Arthur P. Teele acting as attorney for the owners. The asking price was $300,000, but no offers were known to have been made.

subfiles.title: Singapore telegram on Japanese purchases of Dutch tin
subfiles.about: Reports proposals for American forward purchasing of Bangka tin to prevent Japanese acquisitions and possible diversion to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Japanese interests had been buying unusually large quantities of Dutch tin, some believed destined for Germany. British and Dutch officials suggested that U.S. private or government buyers contract three to six months ahead for the roughly 2,000-ton monthly output of the Bangka smelter, avoiding the embarrassment of a formal Dutch restriction.

subfiles.title: Reply authorizing possible Metals Reserve purchases of Bangka tin
subfiles.about: States that Metals Reserve is willing to consider purchasing Bangka tin deliverable before July 1.
subfiles.summary: The Department says Bangka's American agents may offer Metals Reserve all tin deliverable before July 1. Acceptance of later deliveries depends on settlement of the renewal terms for the International Tin Agreement.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Metals Reserve concerning Bangka tin purchases
subfiles.to: President of the Metals Reserve Company
subfiles.about: Asks whether Metals Reserve is interested in the forward-purchase arrangement proposed in the Singapore telegram.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses the December 21 telegram from Singapore. It requests a statement on whether Metals Reserve wishes to enter the proposed arrangement for purchasing Dutch tin.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning licenses for steel exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Robert B. Parkman, secretary to Senator Rufus C. Holman
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's question about alleged shipments of steel ingots to Japan after the scrap-iron embargo.
subfiles.summary: Parkman quotes C. H. Swanson of The Dalles, who asks whether steel ingots are still being shipped to Japan and who has authority to approve or refuse foreign shipments. Parkman requests a report answering those questions.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning licensing of iron and steel exports
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that exports of iron, steel, and scrap require licenses administered by the Administrator of Export Control.
subfiles.summary: Price acknowledges the inquiry arising from C. H. Swanson's letter. He identifies the Administrator of Export Control as the responsible official and encloses presidential proclamations and regulations concerning defense-related exports.

subfiles.title: Shipment of vanadium through Buenos Aires to Japan
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, American Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports the transshipment of nearly five thousand bags of vanadium from Mexico through Buenos Aires to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The S.S. Uruguay arrived with 4,957 bags described as a transshipment from Tampico, consigned by a New York corporation to Sudametal in Buenos Aires. Embassy investigation found Sudametal to be a poorly rated German-Jewish concern, and the cargo was transferred by lighter to the Japanese ship Jamara Maru, which departed for Japan through the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on an arms embargo against Japan
subfiles.about: References a Shanghai telegram concerning embargoes on war materials for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a Navy Department letter containing a copy of a telegram from Shanghai. The underlying subject was the proposed embargo on arms and other war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on raw materials for the Japanese steel industry
subfiles.about: References a Commerce Department memorandum on raw materials used by Japan's steel industry.
subfiles.summary: The cited memorandum was prepared by the Metals and Minerals Division of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. A copy was transmitted to the State Department and filed elsewhere under the iron-and-steel classification.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese agents seeking steel mills and rails
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of Commercial Affairs, Geist
subfiles.about: References information about two Japanese agents seeking steel mills and reusable streetcar rails in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reported Japanese interest in buying steel mills and old streetcar rails from Los Angeles or San Francisco. The proposed rails transaction, which would have included the cost of tearing up streets, was not completed and appeared intended for reuse rather than scrap.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on extraordinary quebracho shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of American Republics
subfiles.about: References a conversation with G. F. Thorold about large quebracho shipments to Japan and possible U.S. purchase.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum concerned unusually large quebracho exports to Japan. It also considered whether the National Defense Commission might purchase the commodity instead.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japan's need for rubber
subfiles.about: References a Justice Department memorandum concerning Japanese demand for rubber.
subfiles.summary: The original Justice Department letter transmitted a memorandum about Japan's need for rubber. The cross-reference directs the reader to file 894.6176/3.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on aluminum for a Chinese rolling mill
subfiles.about: References a conversation about supplying aluminum to a Chinese company that promised not to sell its output to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: F. W. Bilfinger, general manager of Chinese Aluminum Rolling Mills Limited in Shanghai, sought aluminum from the United States. He stated that the company intended to prevent its products from reaching Japan or Japanese interests in China.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Soviet transit of arms and military supplies
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Chungking, Nelson T. Johnson
subfiles.about: References a report on German questions about Soviet transit facilities for American arms to China and German supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Germany reportedly asked whether the Soviet Union had permitted American arms to cross Soviet territory en route to China. It also asked whether comparable transit facilities might be available for military supplies moving between Germany and Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmission concerning the Australian steel and scrap-iron embargo
subfiles.to: Clarence E. Gauss, American Minister, Canberra
subfiles.about: Sends a confidential memorandum of a conversation with the Australian minister about Australia's steel and scrap-iron embargo and American aid.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses the record of his December 3 conversation with the Australian minister. The subjects were Australia's restrictions on steel and scrap-iron exports and assistance from the United States.

subfiles.title: Senator Bankhead's endorsement of a citizens' embargo petition
subfiles.about: Forwards and endorses a Prichard citizens' demand for an embargo on materials useful to Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Bankhead encloses the original letter signed by Gladys Thomas and numerous other citizens. He argues that because Japan has stopped buying American cotton, its remaining purchasing power should not be used to obtain war materials and implements.

subfiles.title: Prichard citizens' petition for aid to China and a total war-supplies embargo
subfiles.from: Gladys Thomas and other citizens of Prichard, Alabama
subfiles.about: Calls for increased financial aid to China and an immediate embargo on all war supplies, oil, and gasoline to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The signers support greater assistance to China and demand that American companies at home or in the Dutch East Indies be barred from supplying Japan with petroleum. They condemn continued sales as complicity in Japanese cruelty, a threat to missions and American business in Asia, and a danger to democracy and national safety.

subfiles.title: State Department response to Senator Bankhead and Gladys Thomas
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the embargo petition and explains that further restrictions under the Export Control Act remain under government review.
subfiles.summary: The Department says Gladys Thomas's letter has received careful consideration and that all interested agencies are continually examining additional restrictions under the July 2, 1940 Export Control Act. It returns the petition and supplies the act, presidential proclamations, executive orders, regulations, White House announcements, and an information sheet on iron and steel products.

subfiles.title: Circular telegram summarizing American press criticism of Japan policy
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, with information copies to Peiping and Chungking
subfiles.about: Begins a review of American editorial reaction to iron-and-steel export controls and relations with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram says recent press commentary has focused on U.S. controls over iron and steel exports, Japan's relations with the South Seas, and public statements by Japan's foreign minister and the American ambassador. It quotes the Christian Science Monitor and Philadelphia newspapers as arguing that American restrictions had been moderate and might need to be extended if Japanese aggression continued. The telegram continues beyond page 400.
